title: Unborn, beyond the elements
hook: ajoo hain, abhoo hain: never born, not made of earth or water (Jaap, chachari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, formless, aroop hain, anoop hain, and your line, beyond compare. Did you leave a comparison unfinished? Today, the next two short lines of the chachari. Day three hundred forty.

Everything you've ever touched was made of something. The table: wood, which was a tree, which was soil and rain and light. Your coffee: water, beans, heat. Your own body: about sixty percent water, plus minerals that were once in the ground, plus the air in your lungs right now. Even you had a birthday. A day, a place, a mother. Everything has a when it began and a what it's made of. Jaap Sahib names something that has neither. Today: unborn, beyond the elements.
screen: `THE TABLE WAS A TREE.` → `YOUR BODY: WATER, MINERALS, AIR.` → `EVERYTHING HAS A BIRTHDAY.`

segments.voice: The two-word lines keep coming. Ajoo hain. Abhoo hain. Start with the first. Joon is a Punjabi word for a birth, a life-form, a body you're born into. Ajoo, and its fuller form ajooni, means not born into any form. Never born. If that word sounds familiar, it should. It's in the Mool Mantar, Guru Nanak's words that open the Guru Granth Sahib, the lines many Sikhs learn first: ajooni saibhang, unborn, self-existent. Guru Arjan set them at the head of the scripture when he compiled it in 1604, and here the Tenth Guru brings the idea back, nearly two centuries after Guru Nanak, in his own morning praise. The first Guru and the tenth, saying the same thing in different meters. Then abhoo. Bhoo is the earth, the ground, the stuff things are made of. Abhoo: not made of earth. Sikh scripture often speaks of the body as made of five elements, earth, water, fire, air and space, borrowed for a while and given back. The One, Jaap says, isn't made of any of them. Not a very large person. Not a force inside the world like gravity. Something that isn't built from the world's materials at all. Sikh teaching holds firmly that the One is never born and never dies, and so is never shaped by any body. On an ordinary day, that matters. Everything you can touch will change, wear out, return to the ground, including your own hands. That can be frightening. Ajooni says that what you bow to is not on that list. Not made of this. Which means it can't wear out.
screen: `JOON: A BIRTH, A BODY.` · `AJOONI: NEVER BORN.` · `MOOL MANTAR: AJOONI SAIBHANG.` · `ABHOO: NOT MADE OF EARTH.` · then, large: `NOT MADE OF THIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch earth and water, then be still. If you can, put your fingers on soil, a plant pot, a stone, or the floor. Feel it: solid, cool, made. Then touch water, a glass, the tap, a damp cloth. Feel it: wet, moving, made. Your hand is made of these too. Now take your hand away, rest it in your lap, and sit still. Let your attention go past what you can touch, to the quiet behind it. If you pray, you can say ajooni softly. The bell holds the time.
Ajooni. Never born into any body: the word from the Mool Mantar that Jaap echoes with ajoo hain, abhoo hain, unborn and not made of earth.
Your line: not made of this. Today, when something you own breaks or wears out, let it remind you: not everything wears out. Day three hundred forty.

screen: `DAY 340 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SALUTATION TO THE ARMED ONE.`

howItsDone: Sikhs say ajooni saibhang every day in the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji, and hear the same idea again in Jaap's ajoo hain, abhoo hain.

fork.setup: the Tenth Guru is writing his morning praise. which earlier Sikh words does he echo in ajoo hain?
options: a line from a Persian poem.
fork.reveal: Guru Nanak's opening lines call the One ajooni, unborn; the Tenth Guru brings it back nearly two centuries later.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ajooni, never born into any body, from joon, a birth; in the Mool Mantar.

trapdoor: what you thought: unborn is just another way of saying very old.
what it means: the One was never born and isn't made of earth, water or any element at all.
what a scholar hears: ajoo and abhoo in Jaap's chachari restate the Mool Mantar's ajooni saibhang; joon comes from Sanskrit yoni, birth or womb.

sources.ref: Jaap Sahib, chachari chhand: ajoo hain, abhoo hain
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Mool Mantar): ajooni saibhang

notes: Ajoo glossed as unborn and abhoo as not made of earth/elements; some translations render abhoo differently (e.g., 'without elements', 'not of the world'). Confirm.
Five elements (earth, water, fire, air, space/akash) as a Gurbani theme: confirm.
'A little over two centuries later' (Guru Nanak's Mool Mantar to Jaap, late 1600s): confirm.
Body water 'about sixty percent' is an approximate adult figure.

Audit (2026-10-01): the teach said Guru Nanak put the Mool Mantar at the start of the scripture; it now says Guru Arjan placed it there when compiling it (1604). 'A little over two centuries' became 'nearly two centuries' (Guru Nanak d. 1539, Jaap c. 1690s), also in the fork reveal. Removed a stock phrase.
